outcome: On 6 Oct 2026 OpenAI posted, in its openai/math repository, a manuscript listed as author 'OpenAI' that claims to prove the Zarankiewicz crossing-number formula for all positive m,n, i.e. that no drawing of any complete bipartite graph K_{m,n} has fewer crossings than Z(m,n); a Lean file in the same repo has a sorry-free main theorem for that statement in the files I read. OpenAI attributes the results to an unreleased internal model. As of 13 Oct 2026 no qualified mathematician has publicly checked this manuscript. Other post-2024 work found is an analogue (K_{m,n} minus one edge, m=5), a different extremal problem sharing the name (Zarankiewicz numbers, LLM-assisted), and a rectilinear multipartite upper-bound paper; none of these moves the question.
problem_asks: Single question over all complete bipartite graphs: is there a drawing in the plane of some K_{m,n} (m,n positive integers) with fewer crossings than the Zarankiewicz number Z(m,n) = floor(m/2)*floor((m-1)/2)*floor(n/2)*floor((n-1)/2)? A 'yes' answer is a counterexample for some (m,n); a 'no' answer means cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n) for every (m,n). Parts: (i) the quantifier ranges over every pair (m,n), so a settlement must cover all pairs, not one dimension or a fixed m; (ii) the upper bound cr <= Z is known from Zarankiewicz's explicit drawing, so the open content is the lower bound; (iii) the statement does not restrict the class of drawings, so any planar drawing counts.

events.what_happened: OpenAI released, in the public repository github.com/openai/math, a preprint titled 'The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs' with author listed as 'OpenAI' (README date: September 23, 2026). Its abstract reads: 'We prove the Zarankiewicz crossing-number conjecture, resolving Turán's brickyard problem. For all positive integers m,n, the ordinary crossing number of the complete bipartite graph K_{m,n} is' followed by the four-floor product. The repository also holds Lean 4 code (lean/OAI/Combinatorics/Crossing/Main.lean, declaration OAI.Zarankiewicz.mainTarget_proof, whose statement is: for all positive m and n, there exists an admissible drawing achieving axisPairs m * axisPairs n crossings, and every admissible drawing has at least that many), a Comparator challenge statement (lean/ComparatorChallenges/BipartiteCrossing.lean), and a Lean doc (lean/docs/165.md at commit adc7f12) titled 'The Harary–Hill and Zarankiewicz crossing-number formulas' which says 'The formalized result proves this equality for every positive m,n and constructs a drawing attaining it.' Secondary coverage places the bipartite manuscript in family 165, 'Exact crossing numbers of complete and complete bipartite graphs'; I did not open the repo index to confirm this.
events.revisions: Repository preprint carries a stated date of September 23, 2026 in its README and citation block; the public release was 6 Oct 2026 (Scientific American: OpenAI revealed the results in a GitHub repository at 6 P.M. EDT; community forum post dated Oct 6, 10:47pm). I used 6 Oct as the first public posting, not the September README date. Whether the manuscript or its Lean file was revised after posting is NOT established: the repo commit history returned HTTP 429, and the 7 Oct withdrawals (three Hodge-theory manuscripts) and 14 revised manuscripts reported by secondary sources are not identified with this family.
events.delivers: If the claim holds: for every positive m,n, cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n), so no drawing of any K_{m,n} has fewer crossings than Z(m,n), and Z(m,n) is attained. Restrictions carried by the formal statement: the lower bound quantifies only over AdmissibleDrawing m n, defined as a ContinuousDrawing (vertices at distinct points of R x R; each edge a continuous path, injective along its length, interior avoiding all vertices) with (a) a finite set of crossing points, (b) every crossing between two edge interiors 'proper' (a local chart makes the two edges look like the coordinate axes), and (c) no point on three edge interiors. crossingCount counts the points of the crossing set. The informal question quantifies over all drawings; the formal lower bound covers the admissible ones only. The formal theorem also asserts existence of an admissible drawing attaining the value, which is the known Zarankiewicz construction realised with straight segments.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim and its Lean chain hold. Not established by my reading: (1) that the imported Lean files supporting the lower bound (about 7 of roughly 100 files in lean/OAI/Combinatorics/Crossing that I read, plus the full import closure) are sorry-free and use only standard axioms; (2) that every drawing covered by the informal question can be reduced to an admissible one without increasing its crossing count; (3) that the human-readable argument in paper.tex / paper.pdf is correct (its sections were not in the text I could retrieve).
events.time_since_posted: 7 days as of 13 Oct 2026. No qualified mathematician publicly checking this specific manuscript found. General reactions to the release exist: Gil Kalai's blog (7 Oct) reports the claim and says the results 'will need to be checked and digested by the mathematical community' and that 'even Lean verification may have issues'; Andrew Sutherland (MIT, quoted in Scientific American) says 'treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified'; Quanta (9 Oct) quotes Johan Commelin that formal correctness 'needs human experts to read the Lean code'. None names this result.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib (version not stated in the files read; imports include Mathlib.Topology.Path and Mathlib.Tactic.Common)

events.directly_checkable: Yes in principle. The attaining object is an explicit axis drawing (vertices on two perpendicular axes, straight segments; the vertical and horizontal coordinates are chosen generically within prescribed intervals). I did not check the Lean build or any drawing by hand.
events.doubts: (1) No named human author or external reviewer; preprint authored 'OpenAI'; the repo's formalization.yaml records review status 'unchecked' at project level (not per entry). (2) Release-level errors: three other manuscripts were withdrawn on 7 Oct after a sign error invalidated an argument in one and the construction used by two dependent papers (Retraction Watch; secondary reports on the reasons). The repo README says 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues.' Quanta (9 Oct) says 'a handful of the Lean statements had technical issues' and quotes Commelin that 'some of the formalizations [appear to] prove weaker statements than what's claimed in the paper' (about the release generally; this result is not named). (3) Formal scope: the lower bound is over AdmissibleDrawing only (see delivers). I did not find, in the files read, a lemma reducing arbitrary drawings to admissible ones with no more crossings; the standard reduction is not visible to me. (4) The lower-bound proof is a multi-file chain. I read the files at the top of the chain (Main, BalancedAxisCrossingCount, BalancedAxisDrawing, AxisCrossingOrder, EvenCrossingLowerBound, OddCrossingLowerBound, DeletionCount) and found no sorry/admit/axiom/native_decide/opaque in them. I did not read OddNormalizedLowerBound, ExpectedTrackGeometry, DrawingDeletion or the rest of the chain, and did not run a build or #print axioms. Per-file: even_successor_crossing_lower_bound gives Z(m,n) <= crossingCount for n = 2s+2; odd_crossing_lower_bound gives Z(m,2s+1) <= crossingCount, with degenerate cases closed by simp. (5) The Lean statement is only a faithful formalisation if its definitions match the question; I read them and they encode the four-floor formula and a no-fewer-crossings bound, but I did not audit every definition. (6) The Zarankiewicz formula has a documented history of flawed proofs: Zarankiewicz (1954) and Urbanik (1955) claimed it; Ringel and Kainen (1965-66) and Guy (1969) found the gap in the inductive step. The new claim is not known to repeat that gap, but the history is a reason for caution. (7) Attribution is repo-level (see ai): the README's statement covers 'the vast majority of results' and names an exception (a zero-free-region writeup); this result is not individually attributed.
events.direction: Confirms the conjectured value: claims that no drawing of any K_{m,n} has fewer than Z(m,n) crossings, i.e. answers Turán's question 'no' for all m,n. It provides no counterexample.
events.object: No counterexample. The object exhibited is the known Zarankiewicz-type axis drawing attaining Z(m,n) (vertices on two perpendicular axes, straight edges), realised as an admissible drawing whose coordinates are chosen generically within prescribed intervals. The existence of such a generic choice is proved via the lemma nonempty_balancedAxisRealization, so the attaining drawing is existential in the formal development. The substantive content is the lower bound crossing_lower_bound (for every admissible drawing, crossingCount >= axisPairs m * axisPairs n).

systems.name: an unreleased internal OpenAI model
systems.what_it_did: Per the repo's own description, the manuscripts and proof artifacts were 'produced by an internal OpenAI model'; the release post calls it 'an internal frontier model'. The README says 'The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model'. This manuscript is listed with author 'OpenAI' and no named human; its visible text has no separate production statement, and the repo does not individually name this result in the attribution. Per the repo's exception list, only the zero-free-region writeup was human-edited for readability. The Lean formalisation is recorded as automation 'agent' at project level in formalization.yaml.
systems.basis_quote: The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model.

ai.disclosed_cost: Per the repo README: 'On average, each result used three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute with that model.' and 'Over the course of the evaluation, the model was posed approximately 4,000 problems.' The release post gives the same compute figure as 'equivalent to roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking with the internal model'.

events.what_happened: Bhan, Nobili and Langer posted arXiv 2605.01120, 'New Bounds for Zarankiewicz Numbers via Reinforced LLM Evolutionary Search' (v1 1 May 2026; v3 25 Aug 2026). It is about the Zarankiewicz NUMBER Z(m,n,s,t) (the maximum number of edges in an m-by-n bipartite graph with no K_{s,t}), not crossings. It reports exact values Z(11,21,3,3)=116, Z(11,22,3,3)=121, Z(12,22,3,3)=132 and lower bounds for 41 others, obtained with OpenEvolve, 'an open-source evolutionary algorithm based on Large Language Models (LLMs)'. The paper does not name a model (as read). Recorded as a discarded event: a different problem sharing a name. No AI involvement in this problem is found in this event.
events.revisions: v1 1 May 2026; v3 25 Aug 2026 (per arXiv page).
events.delivers: Concerns Z(m,n,s,t), the Zarankiewicz number for K_{s,t}-free bipartite graphs. It does not bear on the crossing number of K_{m,n}.
events.remains: All of this problem (no crossing-number content).
events.time_since_posted: 5 months as of 13 Oct 2026; not about this problem
events.doubts: None relevant to this problem. Discarded: a different extremal problem sharing the name 'Zarankiewicz'.
events.direction: Not about the crossing number; does not bear on whether any drawing beats Z(m,n).

events.what_happened: Löfberg and Qi, 'Second Order Zarankiewicz Number' (arXiv 2608.30555, v1 31 Aug 2026, v3 13 Sep 2026). About a second-order Zarankiewicz number for biquadratic forms. Not about crossings and not mentioned by any OpenAI material. Discarded: different problem sharing the name.
events.delivers: A second-order Zarankiewicz number z2(m,n) for irreducible doubly simple biquadratic forms, with a hierarchy among related parameters and exact small values. No crossing-number content.

events.what_happened: Brosch and Polak, 'New lower bounds on crossing numbers of K_{m,n} from semidefinite programming' (arXiv 2206.02755, v1 6 Jun 2022; v2 13 Oct 2023 revised after referee comments, stated to be accepted in Mathematical Programming). Lower bounds for fixed m: cr(K_{10,n}) >= 4.87057n^2 - 10n, cr(K_{11,n}) >= 5.99939n^2 - 12.5n, cr(K_{12,n}) >= 7.25579n^2 - 15n, cr(K_{13,n}) >= 8.65675n^2 - 18n.
events.revisions: v1 6 Jun 2022; v2 13 Oct 2023 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Moves a lower bound (not the exact value) for m = 10, 11, 12, 13 and all n. Each bound stays below the conjectured Z(m,n) (which grows like 5n^2 for m=10, by my arithmetic), so it does not establish the question for any m, n.
events.remains: Whether cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n) for every pair (m,n), including all m >= 10 and all of m = 7, 8, 9 for large n.

checked_by.who: Referees and editors of Mathematical Programming
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper after referee comments (per the arXiv v2 comment as read)

events.direction: Partial: lower bounds only; the question is neither confirmed nor refuted.

events.what_happened: Balogh, Lidický, Norin, Pfender, Salazar and Spiro, 'Crossing numbers of complete bipartite graphs', Procedia Computer Science 223 (2023) 78-87, doi 10.1016/j.procs.2023.08.216. Flag-algebra asymptotic lower bounds: cr(K_{n,n}) >= 0.9118 * Z(n,n) + o(n^4); rectilinear crossing number >= 0.987 * Z(n,n) + o(n^4); a local-restriction result. Source details come from search snippets; the DOI page returned only a redirect and I did not open the article.
events.delivers: Asymptotic lower bound for the square case K_{n,n} as n grows: 0.9118 times Z(n,n). Lower bound only.
events.remains: Exact value of cr(K_{n,n}) for every n, and every K_{m,n}.

checked_by.who: Scientific committee of the XII Latin-American Algorithms, Graphs and Optimization Symposium (LAGOS), whose proceedings Procedia Computer Science publishes
checked_by.what_they_did: Peer review of the proceedings paper (per the search snippet's statement; not opened)

events.doubts: Source details are from a search snippet; I did not open the article. A search snippet reports a different rectilinear figure (0.973) from a separate 'Closing in on Hill's conjecture' note; I did not verify which is later.
events.direction: Partial: asymptotic lower bounds for the square and rectilinear cases; the question is not settled either way.

events.what_happened: Staš and Timková, 'The crossing number of K_{5,n} without one edge', Communications in Combinatorics and Optimization, available online 1 Sep 2025 (per the journal page as read; a search snippet gave 4 Sep 2025). They establish the conjectured crossing number of K_{m,n} minus one edge for m = 5 and all n. The authors state their techniques could extend to m >= 6, which the page does not claim as proven.
events.delivers: Establishes the conjectured value of cr(K_{5,n} minus an edge) for all n. Concerns K_{m,n} minus an edge, a different graph from K_{m,n}; does not settle the full question for m = 5.
events.remains: The full cr(K_{m,n}) for all m, n (including m = 5 itself) and the K_{m,n} minus edge case for m >= 6.

checked_by.who: Referees and editors of Communications in Combinatorics and Optimization
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (per journal page)

events.doubts: Analogue (K_{m,n} minus an edge), so it is about a different question; discarded for this bullet's scope. The journal page gives only the online date; I did not see received or accepted dates on the page as read.
events.direction: Confirms an analogue of the conjecture for m = 5 (minus one edge). Does not address the question as stated.

events.what_happened: Fabila-Monroy, Paul, Viafara-Chanchi and Weinberger, 'On the rectilinear crossing number of complete balanced multipartite graphs and layered graphs' (arXiv 2404.13155, v1 19 Apr 2024; v2 9 Jan 2025). The abstract gives upper bounds on the rectilinear crossing numbers of balanced complete r-partite graphs K_n^r and layered graphs L_n^r. The fetched abstract page does not mention K_{m,n}; a search snippet of the full text attributes to the paper a rectilinear-versus-ordinary conjecture for K_{m,n} (its 'Conjecture 3'), which I did not verify.
events.revisions: v1 19 Apr 2024; v2 9 Jan 2025 (per arXiv page).
events.delivers: Upper bounds on rectilinear crossing numbers of multipartite and layered graphs. Upper bounds cannot lower cr(K_{m,n}) below Z(m,n), so this event does not bear on the question.
events.time_since_posted: 18 months as of 13 Oct 2026; no engagement found
events.doubts: Whether the paper's Conjecture 3 concerns K_{m,n} is unverified (the fetched abstract page is silent on it; the snippet says so). Either way, a rectilinear upper bound does not settle the question.
events.direction: Upper bounds on related rectilinear numbers; no bearing on the lower-bound side.

events.what_happened: de Klerk, Maharry, Pasechnik, Richter and Salazar, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 20 (2006) 189-202. Asymptotic lower bound: cr(K_{m,n}) >= about 0.83 * m/(m-1) * Z(m,n) for each fixed m >= 9 as n grows, via a semidefinite-programming relaxation of a quadratic program (new bound cr(K_{7,n}) >= 2.1796 n^2 - 4.5n). Found in the Mohar problem list (opened) and a search snippet; the SIDMA article was not opened.
events.delivers: Asymptotic lower bound of about 0.83 times the conjectured value, for each fixed m >= 9 as n grows. Lower bound only.
events.remains: The exact value for every m, n.
events.direction: Partial: asymptotic lower bounds; not a settlement.

events.what_happened: Christian, Richter and Salazar, 'Zarankiewicz's conjecture is finite for each fixed m', J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 103(2) (2013) 237-247. For each m there is N(m) such that if cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n) for all n <= N(m), then it holds for all n; a finite algorithm per m. Not practical (N(5) reported as about 6e1228 in a blog snippet). Read from search snippets only.
events.delivers: Reduces the conjecture for each fixed m to a finite check (a finite algorithm that either verifies or finds a counterexample for that m). Establishes no specific case.
events.remains: For every m, the finite check itself; hence all of the problem.
events.doubts: Read from search snippets; the Cambridge page was not opened. A 2011 talk abstract describes the same line of work.
events.direction: Method result: reduces the question to a finite check per m; no cases decided.

events.what_happened: Woodall, 'Cyclic-order graphs and Zarankiewicz's crossing-number conjecture', J. Graph Theory 17(6) (1993) 657-671, with computer search. Verified the conjecture for K_{7,7} and K_{7,9} (Mohar list, opened). Secondary sources give wider ranges (K_{7,8}, K_{7,10}, K_{8,8}-K_{8,10}) and disagree. The article was not opened; the range is from secondary reports.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for the specific pairs (7,7) and (7,9) (and, per secondary reports, some further small pairs). Settles finitely many instances of a universal claim; no bound for general m,n.
events.remains: All other (m,n), including K_{7,11} and K_{9,9}, which secondary reports identify as the smallest open cases.

checked_by.qualification: Graph theorist; the paper is a refereed journal article
checked_by.what_they_did: Computer-assisted verification for specific K_{7,n} cases

events.doubts: Computer-assisted cases; secondary sources disagree on the exact list of verified pairs; the article was not opened.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for finitely many pairs (m,n) with m or n equal to 7 or 8 (exact list disputed across sources).

events.what_happened: Kleitman, 'The crossing number of K_{5,n}', J. Combin. Theory 9 (1970). Proves cr(K_{5,n}) = Z(5,n), and via the parity argument (Guy) K_{6,n}; i.e. the conjecture for min(m,n) <= 6. Cited in the Mohar problem list (opened); the article was not opened.
events.delivers: Settles the conjecture for all K_{m,n} with min(m,n) <= 6.
events.remains: All pairs with min(m,n) >= 7 (except those settled by Woodall and later work).
events.doubts: The Mohar list gives 1970; some secondary sources give 1971. The article was not opened.

events.what_happened: Zarankiewicz, 'On a problem of P. Turán concerning graphs' (1954), claimed a proof that cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n) with an explicit drawing. The proof has a gap. Ringel and Kainen found it in 1965-66; Guy identified it in 1969 ('The decline and fall of Zarankiewicz's theorem'). The Mohar list gives 1954 and the flaw (opened); the 1954 article was not opened.
events.delivers: Claimed the exact value for all K_{m,n}; the claimed proof does not hold as published. Establishes the upper bound (explicit drawing) for all m,n, which is still standard.
events.remains: The lower bound for all m,n (this is the flawed part).
events.doubts: The original proof has an error in its inductive step (Mohar list; Guy 1969). Some secondary sources say the case m=3 was handled correctly in Zarankiewicz's work. The gap was discovered by others; no withdrawal by the author is recorded.
events.direction: Claimed confirmation; the claim is flawed.
events.object: The explicit upper-bound drawing (vertices on the two axes, straight segments), attaining Z(m,n) crossings.

events.what_happened: Urbanik, 1955, proposed the same formula and explicit drawing independently of Zarankiewicz, with a claimed proof of optimality that is flawed (Wikipedia summary; original article not checked).
events.delivers: Claimed the same exact value as Zarankiewicz; the claimed optimality proof is flawed.
events.remains: The lower bound for all m,n.
events.doubts: Flawed proof per the Wikipedia summary; original article not opened.

events.what_happened: Hernández-Vélez, Medina and Salazar, 'The optimal drawings of K_{5,n}' (arXiv 1210.1988, October 2012 by arXiv number; Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 21(4), 2014). For n ≡ 2 (mod 4) every optimal drawing of K_{5,n} has antipodal vertices; a two-parameter family of antipodal-free optimal drawings of K_{5,4(r+s)}. Read from search snippets.
events.delivers: Structure of optimal drawings for K_{5,n} (a case the conjecture already covers by Kleitman). Does not change the open question.
events.remains: All of the problem; the K_{5,n} case is already settled by Kleitman.
events.doubts: Read from search snippets; arXiv page not opened.
events.direction: Structure of optimal drawings of K_{5,n}, which the conjecture already covers; no bearing on whether a counterexample exists.

disputes.summary: Zarankiewicz (1954) and Urbanik (1955) independently proposed the same formula and drawing; both proofs of optimality were flawed (gap found by Ringel and Kainen 1965-66; Guy 1969). Not a live dispute about the 2026 claim.

The OpenAI release as a whole is contested: critics say it was released without expert review, and the Association for Human Mathematics issued a statement on 7 Oct 2026 (seen only in search results, as a guest post reposted on Terence Tao's blog; not opened). Quanta and Scientific American report that the release's Lean coverage and verification are incomplete. None of these disputes names the crossing-number manuscript specifically, and I did not find a dispute about its authorship or priority.

summary: Ran 40 web searches and opened the primary sources listed in sources[] (the openai/math repository files, the arXiv and journal pages, and the news and blog items marked opened true). Before the 6 Oct 2026 release, the literature gives: partial settlements (Kleitman 1970 for min(m,n) <= 6; Woodall 1993 for K_{7,7} and K_{7,9}, with secondary sources disagreeing on the wider list), a finite-reduction method (Christian, Richter and Salazar 2013), asymptotic lower bounds of about 0.83 (de Klerk et al. 2006) and 0.9118 (Balogh et al. 2023), SDP lower bounds for m = 10-13 (Brosch and Polak, arXiv 2022, journal 2023), and two 2024-2025 papers that do not decide the question (a rectilinear multipartite upper-bound paper, and the Staš-Timková K_{5,n}-minus-an-edge result). The 2026 OpenAI release contains a manuscript authored 'OpenAI', 'The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs' (README date 23 Sep 2026, public 6 Oct 2026), whose abstract claims 'We prove the Zarankiewicz crossing-number conjecture, resolving Turán's brickyard problem' for all positive m,n. I read its Lean main theorem (OAI.Zarankiewicz.mainTarget_proof, lean/OAI/Combinatorics/Crossing/Main.lean), which is sorry-free in the file and delegates to crossing_lower_bound and nonempty_balancedAxisRealization. I read the top of that dependency chain (about seven files) and found no sorry/admit/axiom/native_decide/opaque there. I did not audit the rest of the chain, did not build the project, and did not run #print axioms. The release README attributes 'the vast majority of results' to 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model' and gives about three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute per result; the paper names no human author. No qualified mathematician has publicly checked this manuscript as of 13 Oct 2026: Kalai reports the claim and says results need checking; Quanta and Scientific American quote general verification concerns that do not name it. Revision status is unknown because the commit history returned HTTP 429. The same release contains three withdrawn manuscripts (a sign error in Hodge-theory papers), which are not this problem, and a Harary-Hill / complete-graph result that belongs to another bullet. Where a call was close: (a) date: I used the 6 Oct 2026 public posting, not the 23 Sep 2026 README date; (b) AI attribution: the repo-level statement is not specific to this manuscript, so I recorded it as the authors' account and flagged that it is not individually attributed; (c) formal scope: the Lean lower bound quantifies over 'admissible' drawings (finite crossing set, proper crossings, no triple points) and not over all continuous drawings, and I did not find a reduction lemma in the files read, so I recorded the restriction rather than judging it; (d) the Lean chain: sorry-free in every file I read, but only partly read.
competing_reading: Read against the claim: the manuscript is a single lab's unreviewed output, authored 'OpenAI' with no named human; the same release has already been shown to contain a sign error that broke three papers; the Lean lower bound is over a restricted class of drawings and only part of its dependency chain was read; the attribution is repo-level rather than specific to this manuscript; and the Zarankiewicz claim has a history of flawed proofs (1954, 1955). On that reading it is a claim that remains unverified, and the problem should be counted as open pending a qualified check. Read for the claim: the Lean main theorem is sorry-free in the file read and states exactly the four-floor formula for all positive m,n with an attaining drawing, so if the rest of the chain holds the question is answered negatively (no counterexample) for every complete bipartite graph, which would close the problem rather than merely moving a bound.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A named expert on crossing numbers reporting that they worked through the manuscript's lower-bound argument and whether it holds. (2) A clean Lean build of OAI.Zarankiewicz.mainTarget_proof at a stated Lean and Mathlib version, with '#print axioms' showing only the standard axioms and no sorry anywhere in the import closure. (3) A lemma (in Lean or in the paper) showing that every drawing in the question's sense reduces to an AdmissibleDrawing with no more crossings, or an argument that the formal class suffices. (4) The repo's commit history for the bipartite manuscript and family 165: whether it was withdrawn or revised after 6 Oct 2026. (5) A later paper that cites the result, or one that still calls the problem open and does not cite it.
